newsitem.title: UK: Hepworth sees profits gain despite sterling.
newsitem.headline: Hepworth sees profits gain despite sterling.

text.p: British heating and building materials group Hepworth Plc said on Thursday redundancy costs dragged down profits in 1996 but it predicted earnings growth this year despite the strong pound and rising pension costs.

"I would expect results to move up modestly despite all these issues and challenges...the underlying momentum is there and we're doing the right things to ensure that carries on. Thereafter the worst will be over," chief executive John Carter said in a telephone interview.

Last year, pretax profits dropped 9.3 percent to 67.6 million pounds ($110.1 million), hit by redundancy costs of 6.7 million as the group cut 500 jobs from its 9,000-strong workforce. Pension charges rose 58 percent to 5.7 million pounds.
Sales rose 1.6 percent to 777.8 million pounds, helped by rising exports and recent acquisitions. The company proposed an unchanged dividend of 14.85 pence.
Hepworth shares showed little reaction to the figures, which were in line with analysts' expectations. The stock was down 4-1/2 pence at 254-1/2p by mid-morning on modest profit-taking.
Carter described sterling's strength as "Hepworth's big issue." That, and a 7.5 million pound goodwill write-off, cut equity shareholders' funds by 2.6 percent to 213.2 million.

"We have had 10 months at current parities between the franc, mark and sterling which is something like an 18 percent adverse movement," Carter said, noting that a quarter of Hepworth products manufactured in Britain were exported.

Carter said the problem was most evident at the French heating business Hepworth Saunier Duval, where profits in franc terms rose last year but operating profit in sterling terms dropped 2.4 percent to 28.3 million pounds.

Hepworth, pledging "vigorous" action to cut its cost base further this year, said the underlying outlook was positive, with signs of modest recovery in the British construction and home improvement markets. The continental heating operations were also seeing firmer demand.

Carter said this year's focus would be on geographic expansion and product innovation, chiefly in boilers and pipes. The company recently bought into a Czech firm and was looking at Hungary, Lithuania, Belarus, Russia and more expansion in China.
"We are very pleased with our early progress in China where we employ 200 people and have two factories coming on stream and the prospects of one or two more," he said.
Carter said talks on the possible sale of Hepworth's Refractories Division were continuing.
"We announced this in October. If they weren't promising I think we'd have known about that by now. We're talking to a number of parties and you've got to interpret that positively," Carter said.
In 1996 turnover at the division dropped 3.6 percent to 157.1 million pounds and profits slipped marginally to 7.4 million, weighed down by 3.0 million pounds redundancy and rationalisation costs.
